Casualty data 23 September 2026
This is a static snapshot, generated on 23 September 2026 so that this section of the record can be read, linked and indexed without JavaScript. The charts, maps, filters and search are in the interactive version of this page.
Constituency

649 seats, 6 divisions, 27 petitions, 181 debates

The scorecard holds one row for the United Kingdom, and a state is not a thing anybody can write to. This page cuts the same record along the axis a reader can act on: the seat they live in, the member who holds it, how that member voted each time the House divided on Palestine, what they said when it debated it, how many people in the seat signed the petitions that reached Parliament, and what the two public registers record against their name. Nothing here is an accusation. A vote is a public act, a contribution to a debate is on the record, a registered interest is a disclosure made under the rules and a reported donation is a lawful, published gift; what this page does is put them side by side, which none of the registers does, because each is published on its own.

The divisions

What the House was actually asked

6 times the Commons has divided on a question about Palestine that this ledger can identify. The subject of a division cannot be read off the machine record — the House titles a vote by its procedural form, so the vote on an immediate ceasefire is published as “Amendment (h)” and nothing in the data says otherwise — so each question is set out here in full, with the published counts that identify it and a link to the division list itself.

Proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation

2 July 2025

ProscriptionTerrorism Act 2000 (Proscribed Organisations) (Amendment) Order 2025 · Moved by the Home Secretary

That the draft Order, proscribing Palestine Action alongside the Russian Imperial Movement and Maniacs Murder Cult, be approved.

A vote for it meant: for the proscription
385 for 26 against Approved
In plain terms

This made it a crime to belong to or support Palestine Action, a direct-action group that broke into and damaged sites of Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms maker, and RAF aircraft at Brize Norton, using the same law as for terrorist groups. Since then, people holding signs in its support have been arrested under that law. Because two violent neo-Nazi groups were banned in the same vote, voting “against” also meant voting not to ban them.

The pro-Palestinian side: a vote against. A vote against treating a Palestine solidarity direct-action group as terrorist. Weaker evidence than the others, because of the two groups banned with it.

The Order did not put Palestine Action to the House on its own. It proscribed the group in one instrument with two violent neo-Nazi organisations, so that a member who objected to treating a non-violent direct-action group as terrorist could not say so without also voting to leave the other two unproscribed. A vote here is therefore weaker evidence of a view than a vote on the ceasefire, and the ledger says so rather than counting it as though it were clean.

Of the 645 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 376 voted for it, 28 against, and 241 did not vote.

The division list at votes.parliament.uk

An immediate ceasefire in Gaza

15 November 2023

CeasefireKing's Speech Motion for an Address: Amendment (h) · Moved by the Scottish National Party

That the House call on the government to join the international community in pressing all parties to agree to an immediate ceasefire.

A vote for it meant: for an immediate ceasefire
125 for 293 against Defeated
In plain terms

MPs were asked whether the United Kingdom should call for an immediate ceasefire. A vote “for” was a vote for a ceasefire. It lost by 125 to 293, so the House of Commons did not call for one.

The pro-Palestinian side: a vote for. A vote for an immediate ceasefire.

The first time the House divided on a ceasefire. Fifty-six Labour members voted for the amendment against a whip to abstain, and ten Labour frontbenchers left their posts over it: four shadow ministers resigned beforehand in order to vote for it, four were sacked afterwards, and two parliamentary aides stood down. That is why this division, rather than the one taken with it, is the one the parties have been answering for since.

Of the 293 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 71 voted for it, 83 against, and 139 did not vote.

The division list at votes.parliament.uk

Extended humanitarian pauses, short of a ceasefire

15 November 2023

CeasefireKing's Speech Motion for an Address: Amendment (r) · Moved by the Labour front bench

That the existing daily humanitarian pauses be extended to allow aid in at sufficient scale, as a step towards an enduring cessation of fighting as soon as possible.

A vote for it meant: for extended pauses rather than a ceasefire
183 for 290 against Defeated
In plain terms

Labour’s alternative to a ceasefire: longer pauses in the fighting so that more aid could get in. It also lost. Because supporters of a ceasefire and opponents of one both voted for it, a vote here does not show which side a member took on the war, and this ledger does not count it either way.

Not counted in the pro-Palestinian filter. Not counted: ceasefire supporters and opponents voted on both sides of it.

Taken on the same afternoon as the ceasefire amendment and worded to stop short of one. It is in the ledger because the pair is the point. Of the 183 members who voted for pauses, 62 also voted for the ceasefire and 121 did not vote on it; none voted against it. The 290 against pauses were almost all Conservatives voting down an opposition amendment, not members who wanted less aid.

Of the 293 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 151 voted for it, 83 against, and 59 did not vote.

The division list at votes.parliament.uk

The anti-boycott Bill: third reading

10 January 2024

BoycottsEconomic Activity of Public Bodies (Overseas Matters) Bill: Third Reading · Moved by the Conservative government

That the Bill be now read the third time.

A vote for it meant: for the Bill
282 for 235 against Agreed
In plain terms

The final Commons vote on the same anti-boycott Bill. It passed the Commons, then ran out of time in the House of Lords before the 2024 election, so it never became law.

The pro-Palestinian side: a vote against. A vote against barring public bodies from boycotting Israel and the settlements.

The last Commons vote on the Bill, and the one on which the Labour front bench voted against it. The Bill went to the Lords, was still in committee there when Parliament was dissolved for the 2024 election, and was lost in the wash-up; it never became law.

Of the 293 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 86 voted for it, 157 against, and 50 did not vote.

The division list at votes.parliament.uk

The anti-boycott Bill: second reading

3 July 2023

BoycottsEconomic Activity of Public Bodies (Overseas Matters) Bill: Second Reading · Moved by the Conservative government

That the Bill be now read a second time.

A vote for it meant: for the Bill
268 for 70 against Agreed
In plain terms

The Bill would have stopped councils, universities, pension funds and other public bodies from refusing, on ethical grounds, to buy from or invest in Israel or the illegal settlements. A vote “for” supported that ban on boycotts.

The pro-Palestinian side: a vote against. A vote against barring public bodies from boycotting Israel and the settlements.

The Bill barred public bodies from purchasing and investment decisions influenced by political or moral disapproval of a foreign state, and its clause 3(7) named Israel, the Occupied Palestinian Territories and the occupied Golan Heights as the only places a minister could not exempt by regulation. The vote was taken straight after a reasoned amendment declining the Bill a second reading, moved from the Labour benches, fell by 212 to 272. The Bill itself then passed by 268 to 70 because most Labour members did not vote on it: the division list records 184 Labour members with no vote. On this division an absence was the party’s position rather than a member’s own choice, and is weaker evidence of a view than an absence on the others.

Of the 288 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 76 voted for it, 27 against, and 185 did not vote.

The division list at votes.parliament.uk

Recognising the State of Palestine alongside Israel

13 October 2014

RecognitionPalestine and Israel (Backbench Business motion), Division 54 · Moved by Grahame Morris, from the Labour back benches

That this House believes that the Government should recognise the state of Palestine alongside the state of Israel, as a contribution to securing a negotiated two state solution.

A vote for it meant: for recognising the State of Palestine
274 for 12 against Agreed
In plain terms

MPs told the government, by a large majority, that it should recognise Palestine as a state. The vote was advice, not law, so nothing changed until the government decided to do it itself eleven years later.

The pro-Palestinian side: a vote for. A vote for recognising the State of Palestine.

A backbench motion, which does not bind the government, and the government did not act on it for eleven years: the United Kingdom recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025. Those opposed to the motion declined to put up tellers, so two of its supporters, Jeremy Corbyn and Mike Wood, told for the Noes so that the vote could be recorded by name at all; Corbyn said so from the floor immediately afterwards. The division list therefore names him on the side he opposed, and this ledger shows him as a teller who forced the vote rather than as a vote against. The Commons votes service does not carry a division this old, so it is read from Hansard, which lists only those who voted; a member is shown as not voting only where their own record of service puts them in the House that day.

Of the 129 members who sat in that division and still hold a seat: 66 voted for it, 2 against, and 60 did not vote, and 1 told for the other side so that the vote could be held.

The division in Hansard

The SNP opposition day motion for an immediate ceasefire

21 February 2024
In plain terms

The House of Commons did call for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire that day, but without a recorded vote, so there is no list of who supported it.

No division list exists. Against the convention that only a government amendment is selected on an opposition day, the Speaker selected a Labour amendment as well. The government withdrew from the proceedings, the Labour amendment calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire was agreed without a division, and the motion as amended was then agreed without one, so the SNP’s own wording was never voted on and no member’s position that day is on the record. The only division was a motion to sit in private, moved in protest, which was not a vote on Gaza and is not carried here.

Every seat

The whole House, most pro-Palestinian first

Pick a division and see how every member voted on it, or narrow the list to the members who spoke in a debate on the subject, or rank the seats by how many of their constituents signed a petition. A member who was not in the House for a division is shown as not yet elected rather than as absent, because an absence is a choice and a later arrival is not.

How the bar under each name is measured

Two kinds of act, both on the public record. Votes: the 5 divisions below that have a clear pro-Palestinian side. Signed statements: the 127 early day motions tabled since 7 October 2023 that take a side, out of 175 on the subject that were each read in full. An early day motion is a short statement MPs sign to put their view on the record, such as calling for an arms embargo, for recognition or for a ceasefire. 122 take the Palestinian side and 5 take the other.

A member’s figure is what they did with the chances they had: “93 of 131” means 131 counted votes and motions came up while they were an MP and they took the pro-Palestinian side 93 times. The list is ordered by that count, less any acts against. Members first elected in 2024 have had fewer chances, so their second figure is smaller.

What is not counted: motions about Lebanon, Syria or Iran (13), motions about the hostages or antisemitism that take no position on Palestinians (8), tributes without a call for action (9), and motions on other subjects that only matched a search term (18). Speeches are shown in each row but are not scored, because a program cannot reliably tell a speech for a ceasefire from one against it. Not signing a motion is never counted against anyone: ministers and whips do not sign them. A signature a member withdrew is not counted; the signatures the House itself withdrew when it suspended Zarah Sultana on 20 April 2026 are still counted, because the withdrawal was not the member’s own act.

How they voted on the division chosen above
Across every vote with a pro-Palestinian side

Counted over the 5 votes that have a clear pro-Palestinian side — proscription (against), ceasefire (for), boycott bill, 3rd (against), boycott bill (against), recognition (for) — and only the votes each member actually cast. The humanitarian-pauses vote is left out because people on both sides of the war voted for it. Members elected in 2024 have had one counted vote, the proscription of Palestine Action, which is the weakest evidence of the five because two neo-Nazi groups were banned in the same vote; each row says how many votes its count rests on.

Anything else
649 seats
What the labels mean
Voted for / voted against
The member walked through that lobby. The chip says what the vote meant, because “for” an amendment and “for” a Bill can mean opposite things.
Did not vote
The member held a seat that day and is not on either list. That can be a deliberate abstention, a party instruction to abstain, illness or being elsewhere; the record does not say which.
Not yet elected
The member was not an MP on the day, so they could not vote. This is never counted against anyone.
Teller
One of the two members who count the votes for a side. Tellers do not vote themselves, but they are on the side they count for.
Teller, to force the vote
In 2014 the opponents of recognition refused to provide tellers, which would have stopped the vote being recorded. Jeremy Corbyn counted for them anyway so that everyone’s vote went on the record; he supported recognition.
The bar under each name
“93 of 131 pro-Palestinian” means the member had 131 chances to act on the record and took 93 of them on the pro-Palestinian side. A chance is a counted vote held while they were an MP, or a counted early day motion tabled while they were an MP. Green is the share taken for, red the share taken against, and grey the rest. Open a row to see every vote and every motion behind it.

Recognition

Eleven years from the vote to the act

MPs voted for recognition in October 2014, but a vote like that is advice to the government, not law. Petitions for it were debated in 2021 and 2024, a petition against it was answered in 2025, and the government recognised Palestine on 21 September 2025 without asking MPs to vote. Full diplomatic relations, with a Palestinian embassy in London, followed on 5 January 2026. The sequence is set out here from the records themselves.

  1. 13 October 2014
    The Commons votes 274 to 12 for recognition. That this House believes that the Government should recognise the state of Palestine alongside the state of Israel, as a contribution to securing a negotiated two state solution. The division
  2. 11 March 2020
    A petition opens: “Call for the UK government to formally recognise the State of Palestine” — 52,625 signatures by its close. The government replied on 7 July 2020: “The UK will recognise a Palestinian state at a time when it best serves the objective of peace. Bilateral recognition in itself cannot end the occupation. We need to see a negotiated settlement.” The petition
  3. 13 May 2021
    A petition opens: “UK Government to formally recognise the State of Palestine” — 131,239 signatures by its close. The government replied on 8 June 2021: “The UK will recognise a Palestinian state at a time when it best serves the objective of peace. We continue to encourage progress towards a negotiated two-state solution between the parties.” The petition
  4. 14 June 2021
    MPs debate the petition “UK Government to formally recognise the State of Palestine” in Westminster Hall. A petition debate ends without a vote. The debate
  5. 4 January 2024
    A petition opens: “For the United Kingdom to recognise the state of Palestine immediately” — 283,669 signatures by its close. The government replied on 27 February 2024: “We must give Palestinians a credible political pathway and irreversible momentum towards the establishment of Palestine. We will recognise a Palestinian State when most conducive to the peace process.” The petition
  6. 16 December 2024
    MPs debate the petition “For the United Kingdom to recognise the state of Palestine immediately” in Westminster Hall. A petition debate ends without a vote. The debate
  7. 13 June 2025
    A petition opens: “Recognise Palestine as a State and seek immediate ceasefire in Gaza” — 17,800 signatures by its close. The government replied on 1 September 2025: “Since day one, this Government has been clear that we need an immediate ceasefire in Gaza. The UK intends to recognise the state of Palestine by the time of the UN General Assembly in September.” The petition
  8. 12 September 2025
    A petition opens: “The UK Government should not unilaterally recognise a Palestinian State” — 59,098 signatures by its close. The government replied on 16 October 2025: “Our recognition of Palestinian statehood, done as part of a wider global drive for peace, is helping to deliver the opposite of the petition’s concerns, showing why it was the right decision to make.” The petition
  9. 21 September 2025
    The United Kingdom recognises the State of Palestine. Announced by the Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, alongside Canada and Australia, eleven years after the Commons voted 274 to 12 for it: “Today, to revive the hope of peace for the Palestinians and Israelis, and a two state solution, the United Kingdom formally recognizes the State of Palestine.” Recognition was on the basis of the provisional 1967 borders. A decision of the government under the prerogative; the House was not asked to vote on it. The statement
  10. 5 January 2026
    Full diplomatic relations: the Palestinian mission in London becomes an embassy. The second step, and the one often remembered as the date. The Palestinian Mission in London became the Embassy of the State of Palestine, headed by Husam Zomlot, and the Foreign Office minister Hamish Falconer said: “We welcome the establishment of full diplomatic relations with the state of Palestine.” The United Kingdom kept its own representation as a Consulate-General in Jerusalem rather than an embassy. The statement
Petitions

27 petitions, 2,498,535 signatures

How a petition works: at 10,000 signatures the government has to reply in writing, and at 100,000 MPs consider holding a debate on it. A petition debate ends without a vote, so it cannot change the law by itself; what it does is put the question on the record and make ministers answer it in public. This is every petition to Parliament on the subject that reached ten thousand signatures or was debated, from either direction. A petition is carried whatever it asks for; the ledger does not choose between them. 4 of the debates below were held because a petition passed a hundred thousand signatures. For petitions of this Parliament the signatures are counted seat by seat, and the list above can be ranked by any of them.

The polls

What the public and the governing party’s members said

What people told pollsters, each with a one-line summary. Published polls on recognition, arms and the characterisation of the conduct. Each carries its pollster, who commissioned it, and the population asked, because a poll of one party’s members and a poll of the adult population measure different things.

YouGov for Action For Humanity and the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians · fieldwork 4–5 June 2025 · UK adults, 2,010 asked

More than three times as many people opposed Israel’s actions in Gaza as supported them, and two in three wanted Netanyahu arrested if he came to the UK.

Oppose Israel’s actions in Gaza 55%
Support them 15%
Want the UK to enforce the ICC arrest warrant if Netanyahu visits 65%
Recognise Palestine now 30%
Recognise it eventually 19%
Oppose recognition 10%

Commissioned by organisations that campaign on the question, which offered more answer options than the pollster’s own series and is why the recognition figures are split three ways.

Published 18 June 2025
YouGov for The Times · fieldwork 24–25 July 2025 · GB adults, 2,013 asked

Supporters of recognition outnumbered opponents by about three to one; many people had no view.

The UK should recognise Palestine as an independent state 45%
It should not 14%
Unsure 41%

Published the day the Prime Minister announced that the United Kingdom would recognise Palestine in September unless conditions were met.

Published 29 July 2025
YouGov for YouGov’s own series · fieldwork 17–18 September 2025 · GB adults

Just before the government acted, supporters of recognition still outnumbered opponents by more than two to one.

The UK should recognise Palestine as an independent state 44%
It should not 18%
Unsure 37%

Taken in the week before recognition. Opposition rose by four points on July, and was highest among Conservative and Reform UK voters.

Published 19 September 2025
Survation for Save the Children, Christian Aid and Medical Aid for Palestinians · fieldwork 22–26 May 2026 · Labour Party members (LabourList readers), 1,036 asked

Most members of the party in government wanted it to go further than it had: nearly four in five backed a full arms embargo.

Support an arms embargo on Israel, including F-35 parts 78%
Back a ban on trade with the illegal settlements 87%
Back suspending the UK-Israel trade agreement 68%
Disapprove of the government’s approach to Palestine 62%
Approve of it 19%

A poll of one party’s members, drawn from readers of a party website and weighted to the party’s own contests. It measures what the governing party’s membership wanted, not what the public did.

Published 5 June 2026
YouGov for The Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu) · fieldwork 2–3 July 2026 · GB adults, 2,125 asked

Half of British adults said Israel is committing genocide in Gaza; fewer than one in five said it is not.

Israel is committing genocide in Gaza 50%
It is not 17%
The UK should no longer consider Israel an ally 55%
It should 15%
Support a ban on trade with the settlements 48%

Among 2024 Labour voters, 67 per cent said Israel is committing genocide, 62 per cent backed the settlement trade ban and 72 per cent supported suspending arms sales to Israel. Recorded in the report at §15.10.

Published 7 July 2026
The money

What the Electoral Commission has published

Organisations that campaign on Israel’s behalf are lawful donors and their gifts are lawfully reported. £128,923 of the total in this ledger went to parties and party units rather than to named members, and cannot honestly be attributed to any one of them.

RecipientReportedDonationsLargest donor
Conservative and Unionist Party £69,350 16 Conservative Friends of Israel Limited
Liberal Democrats £33,573 5 Elnet UK Limited
Advance Together [De-registered 01/10/20] £26,000 2 Mr Gideon Israel

This table is wider than the screen — scroll it sideways to see the rest.

Neither register carries a subject index, so both are searched by donor and sponsor name. The register of interests is searched for \bisrael|\bpalestin|friends of israel|jewish national fund|\bzionis|elbit|\bbicom\b|elnet and the donations register for \bisrael|friends of israel|\bzionis|elnet|jewish national fund|\bbicom\b. An interest or a donation recorded under a name that matches neither is not in this ledger, and the terms are printed here so that the gap can be seen rather than guessed at. The register of interests is only ever the current one: an entry a member has since removed is not served by the API and cannot appear here.

Against the state row

What this seat sits inside

The same conduct, one level up.

The scorecard row for the United Kingdom Part XIII.3 — The United Kingdom What the duty to prevent requires of a state party

A member is not the state and a vote is not a war crime. What a division does record is the position a named person took on a stated question at a stated date, which is the only part of a state’s conduct that a constituent is entitled to put to someone directly.
